sections.rawHeading: 1 · Licensing (GOV — high confidence; a real statewide license that reaches masonry)
sections.title: State licensing and registration
sections.confidenceNote: high confidence; a real statewide license that reaches masonry
sections.markdown: **West Virginia is a genuine statewide-license state — and its license reaches chimney repair work at $5,000+ residential.** STATE LAW: the **West Virginia Contractor Licensing Act — RECODIFIED at W. Va. Code ch. 30, art. 42 (§§ 30-42-1 to -20); former § 21-11 is repealed (§§ 21-11-3, -6, -7, -8 all "[Repealed]" verified on code.wvlegislature.gov Jul 10, 2026)** — run by the **WV Contractor Licensing Board (Division of Labor)**, requires a contractor license for work with total cost of **$5,000 or more residential / $25,000 commercial (§ 30-42-3(d), fetched)** — raised from the earlier $2,500. The statute's definitions (§ 30-42-3) name classifications — electrical, general building, general engineering, HVAC, multifamily, piping, plumbing, residential, and **specialty** contractors — and do not themselves name masonry. **The Board's legislative rule does: 28 CSR 2 (current version effective May 4, 2026; sunset Aug 1, 2031) § 3.25 defines a "Masonry contractor" as one "whose principal business is the installation of brick, concrete block, stone, marble, slate, or other units and products common to the masonry industry, with or without mortar, including the installation of grout, caulking, tuck pointing, sand blasting, mortar washing, pargeting, cleaning, and welding of reinforcement steel related to masonry construction," and § 6.2 lists Masonry among the 17 classifications the Board examines** (alongside e.g. Residential and "Remodeling and repair contractor" — § 3.29: remodeling, additions and repairs to existing structures using two or more classifications where the cost does not exceed $40,000). The rule never mentions chimneys. Chimney rebuild, reline, and repointing at $5,000+ (residential) require an **active WV contractor license** in an appropriate classification (masonry, residential or remodeling-and-repair are the natural fits; which one the Board requires for a given chimney job is not stated in the rule). 2026 SB 553 (Acts 2026 ch. 233, effective June 12, 2026) amends §§ 30-42-7 and -9 to allow transfer of a license to a contractor's qualifying immediate family member; it does not change the threshold. Exemptions (§ 30-42-6) include owner-occupant work and material suppliers; § 30-42-20 makes state licensing exclusive of local licensing. Public lookup: **labor.wv.gov** Contractor Licensing Board / license search. This is stronger than much of the mid-Atlantic norm.

sections.title: What the credential does not test
sections.markdown: Narrower than in no-license states but still real: the WV licensing exams test **contracting/business and trade knowledge** *(exam content not re-read Sep 2026)*, not flue diagnosis or NFPA 211 compliance. A licensed contractor can rebuild a chimney to code without ever being trained to inspect one. Also note the **SWEEP vs REPAIR split**: routine **chimney sweeping/cleaning** falls **below the $5,000 residential threshold** (now even more comfortably, after the raise), so a sweep-only operator lawfully needs **no** state contractor license — while a large *repair* that follows does. The raised floor also un-licenses more of the mid-size repair market (a $3,500 repoint no longer requires the license). Licensing-research batch 2 adds a second hole: **the HVAC technician certification (§ 21-16) excludes from "heating system" "a fireplace or wood-burning stove not incorporated into or used as a primary heating system" (§ 21-16-2(b)(1), re-read Sep 25, 2026)** — so a service call on a decorative fireplace or stove under $5,000 may lawfully need neither credential. Individual certs (CSIA CCS, C-DET; NCSG CCP/CCR) remain the competence signal for the inspection itself.

sections.rawHeading: 3 · Home sale (GOV absence check — article lists Sep 15 + full-code phrase searches Sep 25, 2026: no disclosure statute located)
sections.title: Seller disclosure when a home sells
sections.confidenceNote: absence check — article lists Sep 15 + full-code phrase searches Sep 25, 2026: no disclosure statute located
sections.markdown: STATE LAW: West Virginia is a **caveat emptor** state with **no statutory seller-disclosure article found in the current Code**. On Sep 25, 2026, the official code search (code.wvlegislature.gov, all chapters) returned **0 results** for "property condition", "condition disclosure", "residential property disclosure", "seller disclosure", "property disclosure", "known defects" and "latent defect"; "disclosure statement" (17 hits) and "seller shall disclose" (1 hit) returned only unrelated sections (campaign finance, odometers, structured settlements, cemetery trusts, etc.). The prior draft cited a "West Virginia Residential Property Condition Disclosure Act" in Chapter 36; **the current Chapter 36 (Estates and Property, Arts. 1–13) and Chapter 37 (Real Property, Arts. 1–15) article lists on code.wvlegislature.gov contain no disclosure act** (checked Sep 15, 2026). Its existence and any codified section are **UNVERIFIED — do not publish that Act name or any section number.** Absence as finding (pending a full-code search): no mandatory state disclosure form was located. A Realtor-association **seller's disclosure statement** is reportedly the form in market use, with an "as is" option *(REF, not re-verified; the earlier "buyer can waive in writing" claim depended on the unverified Act and is withdrawn)*. So the chimney is disclosed only if the seller volunteers it. Fraud/active concealment remains actionable at common law. No inspection is mandated at transfer; NFPA 211 Level 2 stays a NATIONAL STANDARD.

sections.title: Consumer remedies and cancellation rights
sections.markdown: STATE LAW: the **West Virginia Consumer Credit and Protection Act (WVCCPA), W. Va. Code Ch. 46A** — especially **Article 6 (General Consumer Protection)** — reaches unfair/deceptive home-repair practices and is enforced by the AG's Consumer Protection Division (with a private right of action). Door-to-door work carries a **3-business-day right to cancel** under **W. Va. Code § 46A-2-132 (home solicitation; buyer's right to cancel)**, with the required cancellation notice at **§ 46A-2-133** — cancellable until midnight of the third business day; notice may be in any written form. Home-improvement transactions have their own rule at **W. Va. C.S.R. § 142-5-3**. Complaints: WV AG Consumer Protection.

sections.rawHeading: 5 · Permits & codes (GOV — medium; State Fire Commission base, local enforcement)
sections.title: Permits and building codes
sections.confidenceNote: medium; State Fire Commission base, local enforcement
sections.markdown: STATE LAW/LOCAL: WV adopts the **State Building Code through the State Fire Commission** — legislative rule **87 CSR 4**, active version effective Aug 1, 2022 (SOS Code of State Rules). That version adopts the **2018** I-codes (IRC for one- and two-family dwellings, IBC), as shown by the 2026 amendment draft, which strikes "2018" and inserts "2024". The **2024 update is in progress, not in force**: notice filed 6/29/2026, agency-approved 7/31/2026, comments received 8/18/2026; as a legislative rule it still needs legislative authorization. *(The 2018 edition is read from the strike-through in the agency-approved draft — DOC; the 2022 final file on the SOS site is a scanned PDF not machine-readable.)* **Enforcement is local** — many rural counties have limited or no building-inspection apparatus, while cities (**Charleston, Huntington, Morgantown, Wheeling, Parkersburg**) run active departments. Chimney relines, rebuilds, and solid-fuel appliance installs are generally permit work where a department exists; in unincorporated rural areas there may be no permit process at all. This state needs the local-variance disclaimer.

sections.rawHeading: 6 · CO law (GOV — high confidence; new construction + rentals, not owner-occupied resales)
sections.title: Carbon monoxide and smoke alarm law
sections.confidenceNote: high confidence; new construction + rentals, not owner-occupied resales
sections.markdown: STATE LAW: **W. Va. Code § 15A-10-12** ("Smoke detectors in one- and two-family dwellings; carbon monoxide detectors" — the State Fire Marshal article; the former fire-code section in Ch. 29 is now shown as repealed) requires an operational **CO detector in any newly constructed residential unit with a fuel-burning heating or cooking source**, in residential units connected to such a newly constructed building, in **one- and two-family dwellings intended to be rented or leased, hotels, and motels**, and in schools/daycares with fuel-burning devices; detectors plug into an unswitched outlet or are hardwired with battery backup (hardwired required in new construction). *(Smoke-detector coverage details not re-read Sep 2026.)* Coverage is triggered by **new construction and rental**, not by resale of an existing owner-occupied home — **no statewide pre-sale CO certificate.** Violation is a misdemeanor with graduated fines: **$250 first offense, $750 second, $2,000 third and subsequent**. A permitted chimney job is the natural moment to add alarms.

sections.title: Solid fuel and environmental rules
sections.markdown: No statewide burn-ban or stove-emission regime. Not a material content section for WV.

sections.rawHeading: 8 · Scam landscape (REF — partial; pull specifics before publish)
sections.title: Scam patterns and enforcement
sections.markdown: The WV AG's Consumer Protection Division pursues home-repair contractors, and the door-knock "we noticed your chimney" pitch is a textbook § 46A-2-132 home-solicitation + WVCCPA violation; unlicensed $5,000+ residential work is separately actionable under the Contractor Licensing Act (ch. 30, art. 42). **Specific WV chimney-sweep enforcement actions: NOT YET CONFIRMED — re-run search before publish.**

story.heading: The story
story.markdown: West Virginia **CONFIRMS the master finding, and does so almost to the letter.** It is one of the few states with a **real statewide contractor license that reaches chimney repair** ($5,000 residential threshold under ch. 30, art. 42 — recodified and raised; re-verified Sep 2026) — a strong-license regime — and, exactly as the correlation predicts, its **sale side is hollow: caveat emptor, with no statutory seller-disclosure article located in the current Code.** Strong on the credential, hollow on the sale. The notable operational quirk is the **sweep-vs-repair split at $5,000**: a sweep-only visit (and now most mid-size repairs) can be unlicensed while big repointing needs a licensed contractor — a clean line the page can teach consumers to watch for. Batch-2 addendum: despite the real license, **"insured" is meaningless at state level** — no liability minimum attaches to it, and the only bond (wage bond, § 21-5-14 — re-read Sep 25, 2026: construction employers must bond to "pay the wages and fringe benefits of his or her or its employees when due") protects employees, not homeowners.
